## Overview

The nicheR Shiny app is a point-and-click interface to the same functions
documented in the other vignettes. It walks you through four steps: building
an ellipsoid, predicting it onto a study area, adding sampling bias, and
generating virtual occurrences. Nothing in the app is required to use the
package, but it is useful for exploring parameter choices before writing a
script, and for building several competing ellipsoids and comparing them
side by side.

Launch the app with:

```{r}
library(nicheR)
run_app()
```

## The About page

The app opens on the About page. Each of the four numbered boxes describes
one step of the workflow and links to the matching package vignette. The
sidebar on the left is how you move between steps once you have started.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: About page, full browser window -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_about.png") -->

Two buttons sit in the header and are available from every page:

- **Save** writes your current progress to an `.rds` file. You can reload it
  later from the Previous session input option.
- **Report** writes an HTML summary of the current session.

Click **START** at the bottom of the About page to move to step 1.

# Step 1: Build

## Providing data

The Build page opens on the **Inputs** tab. Start by choosing one of four
ways to supply your environmental data.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: Inputs tab, input type radio buttons -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_inputs.png") -->

**Background layers.** Upload either one or more rasters (`.tif` or `.rds`,
up to ten files) or a single CSV describing the environmental conditions of
your study area. The two are alternatives, not a pair: as soon as you select
one the other is hidden, and **Clear files** brings both back.

A raster always supports both environmental space and geographic space. A CSV
supports geographic space only if it carries coordinate columns that fall on
a regular grid, in which case the app converts it to a raster for you.
Coordinate columns are recognised by name (`x`, `lon`, `longitude`, `easting`
paired with `y`, `lat`, `latitude`, `northing`) and are excluded from the
variables you can model. If no coordinates are present, or the points are
scattered rather than gridded, the app warns you and continues in
environmental space only. Everything on the Build and Predict tabs still
works, but the geographic plots and the Bias tab will not be available.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: CSV upload with the no-coordinates warning showing -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_csv_warning.png") -->

**Previous session.** Load an `.rds` file saved earlier with the Save button
in the header. The app resumes where you left off, including confirmed
variables, every saved ellipsoid, and their lineage.

**Virtual mode.** Work entirely in environmental space with no geographic
coordinates. You name the variables and define their ranges directly. Use
this when you are simulating a niche rather than modelling a real study area.

**Example data.** Use the WorldClim bioclimatic layers for Central America
bundled with nicheR, which also includes bias layers for step 3. This is the
fastest way to see the whole workflow.

```{r}
# The example data the app loads
bios <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "ma_bios.tif", package = "nicheR"))
```

## Selecting variables

Up to six variables can be used at once. Each row has a checkbox and a
dropdown: uncheck a row to exclude that variable, and use the dropdown to
change which layer occupies that slot. A variable already chosen in one
active slot is removed from the other dropdowns, so you cannot select the
same layer twice. The plot beside the controls updates as you choose, before
you confirm anything.

In virtual mode you instead choose how many dimensions you want and type a
name for each. Blank names default to `var1`, `var2`, and so on.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: variable selectors with three slots, one unchecked -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_variables.png") -->

Click **Confirm** to lock in the selection. The box collapses to a summary
with an **Edit variables** link. If you have not built an ellipsoid yet,
editing simply reopens the selectors. If you have, the app warns you first:
editing clears the ellipsoid, the ranges, and everything downstream.

## Setting ranges

Ranges define the extent of the ellipsoid along each variable. Choose one of
three methods. You can switch methods and change values at any time, then
rebuild.

**Manual** lets you type a minimum and maximum for each variable. Defaults
come from the first and third quartiles of your background data.

**From Data** takes a CSV of occurrence records, or any table with one column
per selected variable, and uses the observed minimum and maximum of each.
Column names must match your selected variables exactly. Once matched, the
observed bounds appear along with **Expand min** and **Expand max** fields
that widen the range outward by a percentage. Negative values shrink it.

**From Stats** builds ranges from a mean and standard deviation per variable,
combined with a confidence level. Defaults are derived from your background
data, but you can replace them with published values for your species. This
is the option to use when you know a species' tolerances but have no
occurrence records, which is the usual situation for rare species.

These correspond to `ranges_from_data()` and `ranges_from_stats()` in the
package.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: From Stats panel with three variables -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_ranges.png") -->

The range lines on the plot follow whatever you type, so you can preview a
range before committing to it. Once an ellipsoid exists, the lines show the
ranges it was built from and hold there until you press **Rebuild**, even if
you move the centroid. Editing the range fields again makes the lines follow
your edits until you either rebuild or switch away.

**Reset to defaults** restores the starting values for the current method.
**Initialize Ellipsoid** builds the ellipsoid and unlocks the Covariance and
Centroid sections. Once one exists, that button reads **Rebuild Ellipsoid**.

## Covariance

A newly built ellipsoid is axis-aligned: every covariance is zero. Adjusting
a covariance rotates the ellipsoid in the plane of that variable pair, which
is how you represent correlated tolerances.

One slider appears per pair, so three variables give three sliders, four give
six, and so on. Slider limits are computed so the covariance matrix stays
valid, and moving one slider narrows the range available to the others. If a
combination would be invalid the app shows an error and leaves the value
unchanged. The rotate icon beside each slider resets that pair to zero, and
**Reset all to zero** returns to the axis-aligned form.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: covariance sliders for a three-variable ellipsoid -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_covariance.png") -->

Click **Set Covariances** when you are satisfied. The section collapses, and
**Edit covariances** reopens it.

## Moving the centroid

The centroid mover shifts the ellipsoid through environmental space without
changing its shape, size, or orientation. Use it to ask what happens if a
species occupies the same breadth of conditions centred somewhere else.

**Reset all** returns the centroid to where this ellipsoid started. For a
copy, that is the centroid of the ellipsoid it was copied from. For an
ellipsoid built from its own ranges, it is the centre of those ranges.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: centroid sliders with one shifted -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_centroid.png") -->

## The ellipsoid library

The library lists every version you have saved. The highlighted row at the
top is the **working** ellipsoid, the one the plots and every later tab use.
Its label shows whether you are editing or viewing it.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: ellipsoid library with three saved versions -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_library.png") -->

Each saved row has four actions:

- **View** loads the version read-only. Ranges, covariances, and the centroid
  are shown but locked, so you can inspect a version without changing it.
  **Return to editing** unlocks it.
- **Edit** loads the version with everything editable, including its ranges.
  Saving afterwards updates that version in place.
- **Add** creates a new unsaved copy, carrying over the covariance, centroid,
  and ranges of the version you copied from.
- **Delete** removes the version and everything derived from it.

**Save ellipsoid** stores the working version under a name of your choice,
then offers to start a new one or finish. If the working version is already
in the library the button reads **Update ellipsoid** and overwrites it.

### Lineage

The **Built from** column records where each ellipsoid came from. A copy
shows the name of its parent; an ellipsoid built directly from ranges shows
**root**.

Lineage is broken deliberately when the geometry changes. If you load a
version, edit its ranges, and rebuild, it becomes a root, because the new
ranges describe a different ellipsoid than the one it was copied from.
Changing only the covariance or the centroid keeps the lineage intact.

Deleting a parent does not delete its copies. They are kept and become roots
themselves, and the app tells you how many will be affected before you
confirm.

## The Build plots

Three tabs sit beside the controls.

**E-space** shows your background data in environmental space with the
ellipsoid drawn over it. The **Pairs** view gives one panel per variable
pair; the **2D** view gives one large panel for two variables you choose.

**G-space** shows the study area geographically. Before an ellipsoid exists
it shows which cells fall inside your current ranges, one map per variable,
updating as you edit the ranges. Once an ellipsoid exists it switches to the
suitable area. The **Show** control lets you move between the two.

**Combined** places an E-space panel beside a G-space panel.

Every plot has an **Advanced Plot Settings** panel below it controlling point
shapes, sizes, and colours, and an **Export figure** button that writes PNG,
PDF, or SVG at a size you specify. The default is a 166 x 166 mm full-page
publication figure.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: E-space pairs view with an ellipsoid -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_build_espace.png") -->

Click **Continue** to move to Prediction.

# Step 2: Predict

Prediction projects a saved ellipsoid onto your background data to produce
suitability surfaces.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: Predict tab controls -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_predict.png") -->

**Ellipsoid Version** chooses what to predict. Pick **All versions** to
predict every saved ellipsoid in one pass, or a specific one. Choosing a
specific version also loads it into the working slot, so the plots switch to
show it.

**Output layers** are four checkboxes:

- **Suitability**, a continuous surface from the ellipsoid
- **Suitability truncated**, the same surface with everything outside the
  ellipsoid's confidence boundary set to zero
- **Mahalanobis**, distance from the centroid
- **Mahalanobis truncated**, the same, bounded by the ellipsoid

At least one must be selected. When you switch between saved ellipsoids the
checkboxes update to show which layers that version has already predicted.

**Advanced prediction settings** holds a truncation level that overrides the
ellipsoid's own confidence level, letting you truncate the prediction inward
without rebuilding.

Predictions are stored per ellipsoid, so predicting one version never
discards another's results. Re-predicting a version clears any biased
surfaces and occurrences derived from the old prediction, since those would
otherwise be stale.

## The Predict plots

**E-space** works like the Build tab, with an added overlay selector once a
prediction exists. Choose a layer to colour the background points by its
values, or **Binary suitability** to highlight only the suitable points. The
**2D** view ignores the selector and gives one panel per predicted layer.

**G-space** shows one map per predicted layer, or a single suitable-area map
when you switch **Show** to the binary view. Before you predict, it previews
the suitable area from the ellipsoid alone.

**Combined** lets each side choose independently. Tick several layers for
either side and the panels subdivide within their column, so the E-space
column keeps its width no matter how many maps you show.

Continuous layers use a viridis palette by default, changeable and
reversible in the settings panel.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: Predict combined plot with two layers per side -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_predict_combined.png") -->

The library on this tab is view-only. Editing happens on the Build tab.

# Step 3: Bias (optional)

Sampling bias weights occurrence generation toward areas with more detection
effort. This whole step is optional: **Skip bias** at the top moves straight
to Generate, and occurrences will be sampled from the unbiased prediction.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: Bias tab with the skip button -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_bias.png") -->

**Upload** one or more rasters representing sampling effort: road density,
distance to water, urbanisation, collector coverage, anything that stands in
for detection probability. With the example dataset, an **Example bias**
button loads the bundled layers.

**Prepare** assigns each layer a direction and combines them into one
composite surface. *Direct* means higher values increase sampling
probability; *inverse* means they decrease it. The NA handling control
decides whether the composite keeps pixels valid in any layer (union) or only
those valid in every layer (intersection). The formula used is shown once
prepared.

**Apply** multiplies a prediction by the composite surface. Choose which
ellipsoid and which prediction layer, and whether the effect is direct or
inverse. Combinations that already exist are skipped, so you can keep adding
without losing what is applied. Note that once bias has been applied, the
result is no longer a probability.

Re-preparing the surface clears everything applied from the old one, since
those results no longer match.

## The Bias plots

**Bias layers** shows each raw layer beside its processed version once
prepared. **Composite** shows the combined surface. **Prediction comparison**
shows the unbiased prediction beside every biased version of that layer, so
the effect of the bias is visible directly. Applying bias jumps you to that
tab automatically.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: prediction comparison, unbiased beside direct and inverse -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_bias_compare.png") -->

# Step 4: Generate

The final step samples virtual occurrence points from a prediction surface.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: Generate controls -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_generate.png") -->

**Number of occurrences** sets how many points to draw.

**Sampling strategy** controls where they fall within the niche. *Centroid*
weights toward the niche centre, *edge* toward the boundary, and *random*
samples evenly across all suitable cells. The centroid and edge options are
what let you simulate species that are common at their optimum versus those
detected mostly at their margins.

**Prediction surface** lists every available layer as a checkbox. Layers with
bias applied appear in orange. You can select several at once and get one
occurrence set per layer, which is how you compare what bias did to your
sample. The app reports which sampling method it will use for each, inferred
from the layer name.

**Strict filtering** removes NA and zero-valued cells before sampling.
Recommended for truncated layers, where zero means "outside the niche"
rather than "very low suitability".

**Advanced settings** holds an optional sampling mask, restricting generation
to a specific area, and the random seed. The same seed with the same settings
reproduces the same occurrences; change it to draw a different replicate.

Occurrences are stored per ellipsoid, and the library shows how many each has
produced. **Download occurrences** writes a single CSV covering every
ellipsoid and layer, with `ell_id`, `ell_name`, and `layer` columns
identifying each set.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: generated occurrences over the suitability surface -->
<!-- knitr::include_graphics("figures/app_generate_plot.png") -->

# Working with several ellipsoids

The library, lineage, and per-ellipsoid storage exist so you can carry more
than one hypothesis through the whole workflow at once.

A typical use: build an ellipsoid from published tolerances, copy it, widen
the ranges on the copy to represent uncertainty in those tolerances, and copy
again with a rotated covariance to represent correlated variables. Predict
all three in one pass, apply the same bias surface to all three, and generate
occurrences from each. The **Built from** column keeps track of which came
from which, and every plot tab lets you switch between them without losing
anything.

Save the session at any point and the whole structure, including lineage,
comes back when you reload it.
